A bray is the loud, harsh, grating cry that a donkey makes — that unmistakable "hee-haw" sound. It is the standard, accepted word for a donkey's call, the same way "bark" is the word for a dog's sound or "roar" is the word for a lion's sound.

If you've ever heard a donkey, you'll immediately understand why this word exists. The sound is not soft or melodic. It is sudden, forceful, rough-edged, and carries far. It almost sounds like the animal is straining to push the noise out. That quality — loud, harsh, unpleasant, and somewhat jarring — is the heart of what "bray" means.

"The farmer was woken at dawn by the bray of his donkey."
The Extended Meaning (Human and Other Sounds)

Here is where the word becomes truly interesting and useful. Because the donkey's bray has such a specific and memorable character, English speakers began using the word to describe any sound made by a person (or sometimes a thing) that has a similar quality — loud, harsh, and grating, in a way that is slightly ridiculous or unpleasant to hear.

The most common application is to laughter. When someone laughs in a loud, uncontrolled, almost donkey-like way — not a gentle chuckle, but a big, honking, nasal burst of noise — you can call it a bray.

"She tried to hold it in, but a bray of laughter escaped her."
"His bray of laughter filled the whole room and made everyone turn around."

It can also describe a voice — particularly a speaking voice that is very loud and rather unpleasant, lacking any softness or refinement:

"He delivered his speech in his usual bray, drowning out any chance of polite conversation."

And occasionally it is used for harsh, blaring instrument sounds, like a trumpet playing too loudly and coarsely:

"The bray of the brass instruments cut through the air."
The One Quality That Ties All Uses Together

No matter how the word is used — for a donkey, a laugh, a voice, or a musical instrument — "bray" always carries the same essential meaning: a sound that is loud, rough, and unpleasant in a particularly undignified or crude way. It almost never describes something beautiful or refined. There is always a slightly comical or unflattering edge to it.

This is why when the word is used for a person's laugh or voice, it is almost always a gentle insult or a mildly unflattering observation. Saying someone has "a bray of a laugh" is not a compliment — it paints them as someone who laughs without restraint or grace.

• Literal (donkeys): Simply the sound a donkey makes. Completely neutral and factual in this use.
  • Figurative (people/sounds): Carries a note of mockery or mild criticism. Used to suggest the sound is too loud, too harsh, and somewhat lacking in dignity.
  • The word works both as a standalone noun ("a bray," "the bray") and with the phrase "a bray of" followed by what is being described ("a bray of laughter," "a bray of voices").
A bray is the loud, harsh, grating cry of a donkey — and by extension, any sound (especially a laugh or voice) that shares that same rough, undignified, jarring quality.
